# The Water Cycle

The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between the land, the oceans and the air. Energy from the sun drives the whole cycle. Without the sun, water would stay frozen or still.

## Evaporation and Condensation

Evaporation is the process in which liquid water turns into water vapor. Most evaporation happens over the oceans, which cover about 71 percent of the planet. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves in a process called transpiration. When warm, moist air rises, it cools. Condensation is the change from water vapor back into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets gather around specks of dust to form clouds.

## Precipitation and Collection

Precipitation is any form of water that falls from clouds, such as rain, snow, sleet or hail. Snow forms when the air temperature is below freezing. Runoff is water that flows over the ground into streams, rivers and lakes. Some water soaks into the soil and becomes groundwater. An aquifer is a layer of rock or sand that stores groundwater. Wells draw water from aquifers deep underground.

There are three main types of precipitation: rain, snow and hail. Hail forms because strong winds carry raindrops high into freezing air again and again. Heavy rain can cause flooding when the ground is already full of water.

## Measuring the Cycle

Scientists use a rain gauge to measure how much precipitation falls in one place. A hygrometer is an instrument that measures humidity, the amount of water vapor in the air. Warmer air can hold more water vapor than cooler air. Rising ocean temperatures lead to more evaporation and heavier storms.

## A Short History of Weather Records

In 1643, an inventor in the town of Lorvale built one of the first barometers to measure air pressure. In 1714, a glassmaker named Pell Varo created a reliable mercury thermometer. In 1802, a pharmacist named Odren Tal sorted clouds into groups such as cumulus and stratus. In 1870, the national weather office of Veloria began daily weather maps. Today, satellites track clouds and storms across the whole planet.
